opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we started in 1998, many people thought it was close to impossible, and in some ways I understood why. China's computer science research then was not where it is today. There were very good universities, Tsinghua, Peking University, USTC, and some extremely talented students, but the research infrastructure, the funding, and the connection to the international academic community were quite limited. Very few papers from China appeared at top conferences like SIGGRAPH, CVPR, or ACM Multimedia.

When I came back from the U.S., where I'd been working in industrial research for many years, a lot of friends asked me, "Why would you give that up? Can you really do world-class research in Beijing?" There was real skepticism, inside Microsoft and outside.

The way I assessed it came down to a few things. First, talent. I was convinced the raw talent was there. The students were hungry, very smart, and very hardworking. What they lacked was the environment, mentorship, and exposure to the frontier. If we could provide that, they could compete with anyone.

Second, focus. We couldn't do everything. We concentrated on areas where we could build depth quickly and where China had a natural advantage, such as multimedia, graphics, computer vision, speech, and natural language, especially Chinese language processing. We wanted to be among the best in the world in a few areas rather than average in many.

Third, culture. I believed this was the most important part. We tried to create an open, flat, very academic culture. Young researchers could challenge senior people, ideas were judged on merit, and we encouraged publishing at the top venues and engaging openly with universities. We didn't want to be just a development center. We wanted to be a real research lab that contributed to the global scientific community.

And fourth, patience combined with urgency. Research takes time, but we also set very ambitious goals. We said we wanted to be a world-class lab, not a good lab "for China." That framing mattered. It set the bar.

So the challenge was big. But I also saw it as a historic opportunity. China was opening up, the internet was coming, and a generation of young people was ready. Looking back, the biggest thing we did right was to believe in those young people and give them the freedom and the stage. Many of them went on to become leaders in academia and industry, and that, to me, is the real legacy.

r001.rationale: The response cites limited research infrastructure, funding, and international connections, plus skepticism about doing world-class research in Beijing. It does not identify the absence of a prior world-class research institute in China as the reason for that uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started in late 1998, I was honestly quite worried. The challenge wasn't money or Microsoft's commitment, it was whether we could attract the right people. At that time almost all the top Chinese researchers in computer science were overseas, at places like Bell Labs, IBM, or in American universities. China's own research environment was still fairly thin. There weren't many role models for doing basic research inside a company in China, and people questioned whether a lab in Beijing could really do world-class work rather than just localization or support.

So I thought about it in terms of three things. First, people. Kai-Fu Lee and I spent most of our early energy on recruiting, flying back and forth, persuading friends and colleagues to return. The pitch was essentially: China has enormous talent coming out of universities like Tsinghua, Peking, and USTC, and if we can bring senior people back to mentor them, we can build something nobody else has.

Second, culture. We wanted to establish a culture of openness and long-term thinking. Publish in top venues, take on hard problems, don't chase quarterly results. That was unusual in China then, and even inside Microsoft some people wondered whether a lab so far from Redmond could stay aligned with the company.

Third, credibility. We needed early wins to show both the headquarters and the Chinese academic community that this was real. Within the first couple of years we had papers at SIGGRAPH, in speech and multimedia, and technologies going into Windows and Office. Once those results came, recruiting became much easier, and the lab started to attract a generation of young researchers who later went on to lead much of China's tech industry.

Looking back, I'd say the biggest judgment call was betting on the talent pipeline. We were confident the raw ability was there. The question was whether we could create the environment to unlock it, and I think that bet paid off far beyond what we imagined.

r001.rationale: The response says China’s research environment was thin and that few role models existed for company research, but it does not identify the absence of a prior world-class research institute in China as the reason for uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I saw it as a tremendous opportunity, but certainly not something we could take for granted. The key question was whether we could bring together outstanding people and create an environment where they could do world-class research. China had a deep pool of talent, especially young people with strong technical foundations. We needed to connect that talent with experienced researchers and the international research community.

A research institute is more than a building or a budget. You need a culture that values curiosity, encourages people to challenge ideas, and gives them time to pursue difficult problems. We wanted researchers to have both the freedom to think long term and opportunities to see their work make a difference.

So I felt optimistic about the talent. The challenge was building the organization and culture around it. Our ambition had to be to contribute at the highest international level.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes building the organization and culture as challenging, but does not say that China lacked a prior world-class research institute or connect that absence to uncertainty about whether one could be built.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, the biggest question was whether we could create an environment in China where world-class research could flourish. There were many talented students and researchers, but talent alone was not enough. We needed a strong research culture, excellent leadership, and the freedom to pursue ideas with a long-term perspective.

I felt the challenge was significant, but the opportunity was even greater. We had to connect China’s talent with the international research community, set a very high standard, and give people the resources and trust to do their best work. The goal was to build a lab in China that would contribute at the highest level globally.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about creating the right research environment, but does not identify the absence of a prior world-class research institute in China as the reason.
